chunks.document_content: Background Diabetic macular edema (DME) is becoming one of the leading causes of blindness worldwide with a significant impact on quality of life. The effectiveness of intravitreal (IVT) anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) therapy has been established by clinical trials and has become the treatment of choice in the majority of DME patients in reducing macular edema and improving visual acuity. Frequent drop-out and discontinuation of treatment are major issues. Lack of compliance can lead to worsening outcomes and be a burden to patients and the healthcare system.

chunks.document_content: Key messages Diabetic macular edema is the leading cause of vision loss in diabetic patients. Options for treatment include intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents (ranibizumab, aflibercept and off-label injections of bevacizumab) and intravitreal corticosteroids (0.2 μg/day fluocinolone acetonide [FAc] implant, dexamethasone implant and off-label injections of triamcinolone acetonide). IL-6, IL-8, IP-10, MCP-1, VEGF, CD54, PIGF, and PEDF were measured in the vitreous of patients suitable for an FAc implant for treatment of chronic diabetic macular edema. Treatment with the FAc implant led to significant changes in inflammatory and angiogenic vitreous cytokine levels in IL-6, IP-10, MCP-1 and CD54. The use of the FAc implant for treatment of diabetic macular edema also improves clinical parameters, as evidenced by the reduction of macular edema on OCT. of corticosteroid over a 3-year period [2], meaning that other preparations have a limited durability of release compared to the FAc implant [9].

In contrast, Lee et al.28 found that a thicker ORL and thicker central macular thickness was correlated with better visual acuity in preschool age children with a history of prematurity compared to full-term born chil-dren. In BabySTEPS, we evaluated visual acuity in prema-ture infants at nine months' corrected age and found that retinal nerve fiber layer thinning across the papillomacular bundle and prior ROP treatment are associated with poorer grating visual acuity.41 Increased foveal total retinal thick-ness, but not inner retinal thickness or inner nuclear layer thickness, was associated with poorer nine-month visual acuity, but the association was only significant in univari-able analysis, although outer retinal layer thickness was not assessed.41 In addition, macular edema is a common and often self-resolving finding in preterm infants, found in up to approximately 60% of preterm infants, yet its func-tional significance is not well understood.6,9,21,23,41-43 Prior studies have reported mixed results regarding its impact, with some studies showing reduced visual acuity, poorer neurodevelopmental outcomes and others showing no asso-ciation with visual acuity.40,41,44-46 In our study, we found that infants with a history of macular edema had signifi-cantly thicker ORL compared to infants without a history of macular edema. These findings may suggest that there is likely a complex interplay between prematurity, foveal morphology, macular edema and functional outcomes, high-lighting the need for further research to elucidate these findings.
